client: I've been really struggling since I got promoted at work last month. The new responsibilities feel crushing, and I keep worrying that I'm not qualified enough for this position. I lie awake at night going over every small mistake, convinced my boss will realize they made a mistake in promoting me.
therapist: It sounds like this promotion has brought up a lot of self-doubt and anxiety for you. Let's explore together - when you think "I'm not qualified enough," what evidence supports that thought, and what evidence might challenge it?

client:
I get what you're saying about looking at evidence, but it's hard to even consider the positive stuff when I feel this way. The truth is I only got this promotion because my manager left suddenly - it's not like I actually earned it through skill. And now everyone's watching me and waiting for me to fail. 

Even when I try to list my qualifications, my mind just counters with "but that one project went badly last year" or "remember when you made that mistake in the presentation." It's like my brain won't let me feel good about anything.
therapist: I hear how strongly your mind holds onto these negative examples while dismissing your accomplishments. That self-critical voice can feel so convincing in the moment. Would you be willing to explore how we might gently challenge that pattern together?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard because when I try to focus on accomplishments, my brain immediately counters with "but that wasn't good enough" or "anyone could have done that." It makes me feel like I'm lying to myself when I try to see positives. I just can't shake the feeling that I'm not measuring up, no matter what I do.
therapist: It sounds like your mind has developed a very persistent habit of discounting your successes, which must feel exhausting. What would it be like to notice these thoughts as just thoughts, rather than absolute truths?

client: I get what you're saying about seeing thoughts as just thoughts, but when I try to do that, it feels like I'm lying to myself. The voice in my head keeps saying "You know these failures are real" and it's hard to ignore that. Even when I do have small successes, they feel like accidents or luck rather than something I actually earned.
therapist: I hear how deeply ingrained this self-doubt feels for you - like even when good things happen, they don't feel truly yours. That must be incredibly frustrating to experience. What would it be like to imagine treating yourself with the same compassion you might offer a friend in this situation?

client: I know I should be kinder to myself, but it feels impossible. When I try to imagine treating myself like a friend, it just makes me feel worse because I don't believe I deserve that kindness. It's like there's this voice in my head that says "You wouldn't let a friend get away with being this inadequate, why should you?"
therapist: That self-critical voice sounds so harsh and unforgiving - no wonder this feels impossible right now. I wonder if we could start smaller, perhaps just noticing when that voice appears without needing to change it yet?

client:
I get what you're saying about noticing the self-criticism, but it's hard not to react when that voice shows up. It feels like getting punched in the gut every time - I can't just observe it calmly. 

And honestly, part of me thinks I deserve that harsh voice. If I wasn't so hard on myself, wouldn't I just become lazy or complacent? That's what I'm afraid of.
therapist: It sounds like that self-critical voice feels protective in a way - like it's keeping you from becoming complacent. I'm curious, have you noticed times when being kind to yourself actually helped you perform better rather than becoming lazy?

client:
That's an interesting way to look at it. I guess there was one time last month when I was kind to myself about missing a deadline, and I ended up working more efficiently afterward. But part of me worries that if I'm too forgiving, I'll just keep making excuses for myself. 

It's hard to trust that self-compassion won't lead to slacking off, because my whole life I've believed the opposite - that being hard on myself is what keeps me disciplined.
therapist: It makes sense that this belief has served you for so long - that self-criticism equals discipline. I wonder if we could explore how that harshness might actually be draining your energy and focus, while that one moment of kindness helped you work more effectively?

client:
I get what you're saying about the self-criticism draining me, but I'm worried that if I go easier on myself, I'll just become lazy. That moment of kindness did feel better, but it also made me anxious - like I was letting myself off the hook too easily. 

It's hard to imagine being productive without that harsh inner voice pushing me. What if I lose my edge?
therapist: I hear how deeply connected your self-criticism feels to your motivation and success - that must create such an internal conflict when considering change. What if we gently explored how that "edge" you're worried about losing might actually be maintained through encouragement rather than punishment?

client:
I get what you're saying about using encouragement instead of criticism, but I'm just not sure it would work for me. The fear of losing my edge is real - when I try to be kinder to myself, it feels like I'm letting my standards slip. 

Part of me knows this harsh self-talk isn't healthy, but another part worries that without it, I'll become lazy or mediocre. It's like my inner critic is the only thing keeping me from failing.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tension between wanting to treat yourself more kindly and fearing what might happen if you do - that must feel like walking a tightrope. What if we explored small, manageable ways to test this belief that kindness leads to lower standards?

client: I get what you're saying about small steps, but even that feels risky. If I start being kinder to myself about missing a deadline at work, for example, I'm scared I'll just keep making excuses and my performance will slip. It's like any relaxation of my standards feels like the start of a slippery slope.
therapist: I hear how frightening that slippery slope feels - like any small kindness could unravel all your hard work. What if we explored how self-compassion might actually help you notice and correct mistakes more effectively, rather than ignoring them?
